title: Take-home drug checking as a novel harm reduction strategy in British columbia, Canada

claims.statement: In people who use drugs in North America who tested their drugs (or, in one study, their urine) with fentanyl test strips, themselves at home or with staff at a supervised injection site (2016 to 2023), a result showing fentanyl was followed, by people's own account, by a safer way of using in a minority to a majority of cases, most often using less or going slower, and seldom by throwing the drug away; no study read observed what people then took. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017), of 31 young adults who said a strip had shown fentanyl, 45 in 100 said they then used smaller amounts, 42 went slower, 39 used with someone else around, 36 tried a small amount first (a 'tester'), 10 threw the drugs out, 10 sold them and 7 gave them away; these answers were given at least two weeks later, the results were not checked, and how many used the drugs as usual was not reported. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), staff recorded an intention to use less after 142 of 391 checks before use that showed fentanyl (36 in 100), against 7 of 122 that did not (6 in 100), and an intention to throw the drug away after 50 of 436 (11 in 100) against 10 of 134 (7 in 100); what people then did was not recorded. In a British Columbia take-home programme (2019), asked a standard question (not about their own results) about what they did when a strip showed fentanyl, 217 of 336 answers (65 in 100) described no change, 86 (26 in 100) at least one safer change and 6 (2 in 100) a riskier one (using alone, or using more or faster). Reviews relay a median of 55 in 100 (23 to 75 in 100, seven studies) reporting some safer change, people using as usual because of withdrawal, tolerance, doubt about the result or wanting fentanyl, and evidence that is mostly intentions and self-reports without a comparison group; both reviews include the Rhode Island and Vancouver studies. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Krieger (31 with a positive result): smaller amounts 45%, went slower 42%, used with someone else 39%, did a tester 36%, threw out 10%, sold 10%, gave away 7%. Karamouzian (checks before use): intended dose reduction 142/391 (36.3%; Wilson 31.7–41.2%) after a positive against 7/122 (5.7%; 2.8–11.4%) after a negative, crude OR 9.36 (4.25–20.65), risk difference 30.6 points (Newcombe 23.3–36.3; editors' calculations); intended disposal 50/436 (11.5%) against 10/134 (7.5%), OR 1.60 (0.79–3.26). Klaire (336 answers to standard questions): no change 217 (64.6%), at least one safer change 86 (25.6%; Wilson 21.2–30.5%), riskier 6 (1.8%; 0.8–3.8%; editors' calculations). Kutscher (relayed): any safer change median 55% (range 23–75%), seven studies, eight locations. Maghsoudi (relayed): 43% of 125 people who inject drugs at a US syringe services programme reported changing behaviour, more often when fentanyl was detected (adjusted OR 5.08, 2.12–12.17).

claims.statement: In people who use drugs given test strips or colour test kits to check their own drugs, handing out kits compared with not handing them out: the evidence is insufficient to say whether it causes harm, for example through false reassurance after a negative result, or reduces harm, and the question is disputed. No study read compared people given kits with people not given them on harm or overdose. What was measured shows few riskier responses: in a British Columbia take-home programme, 6 of 336 survey answers (2 in 100) described using alone or using more or faster after a strip showed fentanyl, in answer to standard questions, and the one study comparing overdoses in people who did and did not use strips found no clear difference, in an imprecise estimate (risk ratio 1.20, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.06). But no study read reports what people did after a negative result (the take-home programme asked and did not report it); a scoping review relays people believing that a negative strip means xylazine or that a darker line means stronger fentanyl, one person saying a negative result would mean using a little more, and strips missing carfentanil and other drugs; and at home, strips showed fentanyl in 73 of 265 methamphetamine samples (28 in 100) and 16 of 93 cocaine samples (17 in 100), against 5 of 97 (5 in 100) and 1 of 92 (1 in 100) tested by staff on site, which the authors think more likely reflects how the tests were done than a different supply. Two critiques argue, without data, that frequent positive results without ill effects could breed complacency, that people who want fentanyl may seek a positive result, and that a colour test showing MDMA may be read as meaning a pill is safe; one of them still supports handing out strips with guidance and naloxone. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Klaire: riskier responses 6/336 answers (1.8%; Wilson 0.8–3.8%, editors' calculation), 1 using more or faster and 5 using alone; responses to a negative result asked but not reported; take-home against on-site positivity, crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 points (14.8–30.1), cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), 16.1 (7.1–25.1). Vickers-Smith: nonfatal overdose adjusted RR 1.20 (0.70–2.06), unadjusted 2.06 (1.09–3.89); composite risk-reduction score 0.86 points higher (0.34–1.38) on 0–15. Kutscher (relayed): riskier use in two studies; difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34%. No study reports behaviour after a negative result.

claims.statement: In people who inject drugs attending two rural syringe services programmes in North Carolina and West Virginia (recruited June 2021 to March 2022), recent use of fentanyl test strips was less common a year after the start than at the start, and not clearly different after six months: the adjusted odds of having used strips in the past 30 days were 0.642 times those at the start at 12 months (95% CI 0.447 to 0.923; all 541 people) and 0.557 times (0.364 to 0.853) in the 212 who answered all three surveys, and 0.936 times (0.696 to 1.258) at 6 months, while the share of those 212 who had ever used strips rose from 65 to 80 in 100. The share using strips at each survey is not printed, so the size of the fall cannot be given as a number out of 100. 213 of the 541 gave no follow-up and had used strips less often, which could bias the trend, and why use fell was not measured (the authors suggest that a test for fentanyl alone tells people less once fentanyl is expected). Over a few weeks, young adults in a Rhode Island pilot used a median of 3 of the 10 strips they were given (10 of 81 used all ten); in that pilot and in a British Columbia take-home programme, 95 or 96 in 100 said they would use strips again, an intention rather than a measure of use. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Past-30-day use, adjusted odds ratios against baseline (mixed-effects logistic regression): 12 months 0.642 (0.447–0.923; 541 people, 1081 observations) and 0.557 (0.364–0.853; 212 complete cases, 636 observations); 6 months 0.936 (0.696–1.258) and 0.946 (0.650–1.375). Lifetime use among complete cases 65.1% at baseline, 77.8% at 6 months and 79.7% at 12 months. No follow-up: 213 of 541 (39.4%, editors' calculation), who had less often used strips (54.3% against 65.1%). Krieger: median 3 strips (IQR 1–6) within a few weeks; 10 of 81 used all ten; 77/81 (95%) would like to use strips in future. Klaire: 322/336 answers (95.8%) would use strips again.

claims.statement: In laboratory tests of urine fentanyl test strips on dissolved samples that contained no fentanyl, compared with laboratory analysis or known content, strips sometimes read positive, mostly with strong solutions of a few other drugs. Among 104 police-seized samples without fentanyl by earlier GC/MS, one brand (BTNX Rapid Response) read positive in 6 (1 of 52 in one laboratory, 5 of 52 in the other; specificity 94.2%, editors' Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, so about 6 in 100 read falsely positive); the five described held only buprenorphine, heroin (two), methamphetamine or noscapine, and because the GC/MS methods were less sensitive than the strip, some may have held traces of fentanyl (Green et al., 2020). In solutions made in the laboratory, strong concentrations of four substances turned the strip positive with no fentanyl present: methamphetamine, MDMA, diphenhydramine and lidocaine. With one strip per concentration, solutions of one seized methamphetamine sample, one seized MDMA sample and retail diphenhydramine tablets and capsules read positive by eye above about 2 mg/mL of material and, by image analysis, from 1 to 2.5 mg/mL, while seized cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products read negative up to 20 mg/mL (Lockwood et al., 2021). With pure standards and duplicate strips on five lots, the thresholds for lots obtained in 2017 and in 2021 were 5 and 10 mg/mL for d-methamphetamine, 50 and 2.5–5 mg/mL for MDMA, 100 and 2.5 mg/mL for lidocaine and 100 and 0.5–1 mg/mL for diphenhydramine, while l-methamphetamine (25 mg/mL), cocaine and ketamine (25 mg/mL) and levamisole (up to 100 mg/mL) did not react (Halifax et al., 2024). Twelve other drugs, among them amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, MDMA and methamphetamine, gave no false positive on four brands at 100 or 1000 ng/mL, and ascorbic acid (vitamin C) at 10 mg/mL or more did so on one brand only (Bergh et al., 2021). The concentrations that gave false positives (0.5 mg/mL and above) were 1,000 to 25,000 times those at which strips detect fentanyl (20 to 500 ng/mL; editors' comparison). Outside the laboratory, people testing at home reported fentanyl in 73 of 265 crystal methamphetamine samples and 16 of 93 cocaine samples, against 5 of 97 and 1 of 92 other samples tested on site by staff, which the authors attribute mostly to false positives from how samples were prepared at home (Klaire et al., 2022; different samples, nothing confirmed, not tested). A scoping review lists cocaine, gabapentin, alprazolam and buprenorphine-naloxone among causes of false positives, citing Lockwood et al., who found these negative (Kutscher et al., 2024). How often false positives happen in real use, and whether a stimulant mixed with fentanyl changes the reading, were not measured; ways of preparing samples that authors proposed to avoid false positives were not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Green et al.: specificity 98.1% (51/52) and 90.4% (47/52); 6/104 false positives (5.8%; specificity 94.2%, Wilson 95% CI 88.0–97.3%, editors' calculation). Lockwood et al. (weighed material, not pure drug; one strip per concentration): by eye above about 2 mg/mL; by image analysis diphenhydramine capsules 1, methamphetamine 1.5, MDMA 2, diphenhydramine tablets 2.5 mg/mL (about 0.10 and 0.25 mg/mL of diphenhydramine HCl, editors' calculation on the card); negative up to 20 mg/mL: cocaine and alprazolam, gabapentin and buprenorphine-naloxone products. Halifax et al. (pure standards; 2017 lots against 2021 lots): d-methamphetamine 5 against 10; MDMA 50 against 2.5–5; lidocaine 100 against 2.5; diphenhydramine 100 against 0.5–1 mg/mL; l-methamphetamine negative at 25 mg/mL; cocaine and ketamine negative at 25 mg/mL (2017 lots); levamisole none to 100 mg/mL (2021 lots). Bergh et al.: 12 non-fentanyl drugs negative at 100 and 1000 ng/mL on four brands; ascorbic acid 10 mg/mL or more positive on One Step only; heroin 50 000 ng/mL no effect. Klaire et al. (different samples, unconfirmed): crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) at home against 5/97 (5.2%) on site; cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%).

claims.statement: In British Columbia in 2019, take-home testing by people who use drugs (strips from ten harm-reduction sites; 218 people returning 336 result sheets) compared with on-site testing of other samples by trained staff at the same sites in the same four months was associated with a similar share of fentanyl-positive results for opioid samples and a much larger share for stimulant samples. Opioids: 994 of 1105 take-home results positive (90.0%) against 591 of 663 on site (89.1%), a difference of 0.8 percentage points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9) within the pre-set equivalence margin of ±5 points. Crystal methamphetamine: 73 of 265 (27.6%) against 5 of 97 (5.2%); cocaine: 16 of 93 (17.2%) against 1 of 92 (1.1%); the study was not powered for these. No sample was tested both at home and on site and nothing was confirmed in a laboratory, so these are shares of positive results, not accuracy; the authors nonetheless conclude that people can use the strips accurately with minimal training, and think the stimulant excess mostly reflects false positives from how samples were prepared at home, which was not tested (Klaire et al., 2022). Results were self-reported, about 6 in 10 sheets were filled in from memory at return (by the paper's Table 3; its text gives the reverse), the number of kits handed out and not returned is unknown, and similar shares near 90% can hide reading errors in both directions. A scoping review relays from other studies that 3% to almost 34% of people had difficulty interpreting results and that some believed the line's strength showed how strong the fentanyl was (Kutscher et al., 2024, second-hand; its figure of positives five times more frequent at home is this same study); a 2018 commentary relays a preliminary study in which 7 of 70 samples gave erroneous or invalid results (McGowan et al., 2018, second-hand); and in a laboratory study of a colour kit, two testers new to it misread known drugs in both directions (Murray et al., 2003). Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
claims.magnitude: Opioids: take-home 994/1105 (90.0%) against on-site 591/663 (89.1%); difference 0.8 points (95% CI −2.3 to 3.9), equivalent within ±5 (p = 0.00275). Crystal methamphetamine 73/265 (27.6%) against 5/97 (5.2%), difference 22.4 (14.8 to 30.1); cocaine 16/93 (17.2%) against 1/92 (1.1%), difference 16.1 (7.1 to 25.1). Second-hand: difficulty interpreting results 3% to almost 34% (Kutscher et al.); 7 of 70 erroneous or invalid results in a preliminary study (McGowan et al.).

claims.statement: In people who use drugs in North America who were offered fentanyl test strips (studies from 2016 to 2023), how many used them varied widely with the setting and with what was counted. In a Rhode Island research pilot (2017) that gave 93 young adults ten strips each, with training and naloxone, and paid them to come back, 62 of the 81 who returned at least two weeks later said they had used at least one (77 in 100; 62 of all 93, or 67 in 100, editors' calculation), a median of 3 strips, and 10 had used all ten; 58 in 100 had given strips to others. At a Vancouver supervised injection site (2016 to 2017), where staff offered a check to every client, about 1 in 100 visits included one (1,411 of 134,176 visits, by an unknown number of people). At US harm-reduction sites that hand out strips (2023), 414 of 732 clients (57 in 100) said they had used strips in the past 30 days. A scoping review of 91 studies to March 2023 relays documented use from 1 to 80 in 100 (median 19), against stated willingness of 43 to 85 in 100; it includes the Rhode Island pilot. A British Columbia take-home programme did not count the kits it handed out, so its rate of use is unknown. Use was self-reported or recorded by services, and was not checked. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: Rhode Island pilot: 62/81 analysed used at least one strip (76.5%; Wilson 95% CI 66.2–84.4%, editors' calculation); 62/93 given strips (66.7%; 56.6–75.4%, editors' calculation); median 3 strips (IQR 1–6); 10 (12%) used all ten; 58% gave strips to others (denominator not stated). Vancouver supervised injection site: 1,411 checks in 134,176 visits (1.05%, editors' calculation), 7 July 2016 to 21 June 2017; the printed average of 533 visits a day does not fit the total, so the share is about 1% or less. Strip-distributing sites, 2023: 414/732 (56.6%) reported past-30-day use at baseline. Scoping review (relayed, unappraised): documented use 1–80% (median 19%); willingness 43–85% (five studies).
